title: Rudraksha mukhi types: a beginner's guide to traditional meanings
description: What mukhi means, how to count the lines on a rudraksha bead, and the deities traditionally linked with 1 to 14 mukhi beads, explained for beginners.
intro: A mukhi is a natural line running from one end of a rudraksha bead to the other, and the number of these lines gives the bead its name: a bead with five lines is a five mukhi, one with seven is a seven mukhi, and so on. Each count is traditionally linked with a particular deity. This guide walks through how to count mukhis, what the common associations are, and how to read seller claims with a clear head.

sections.heading: How to count the mukhis on a bead
paragraphs: Hold the bead so the hole (or the point where a hole would go) faces up. Look for the deep grooves that run all the way from the top to the bottom, like the segments on a peeled orange. Count only the lines that travel the full length. Shallow cracks, scratches or lines that fade halfway do not count.

Turn the bead slowly under good daylight and mark your starting line with your thumbnail so you do not count it twice. On smaller beads a magnifying glass helps. If two people count the same bead and get different numbers, it is usually because one of them included a partial line.

sections.heading: One to seven mukhi: the traditional associations
paragraphs: The pairings below are the ones most commonly mentioned in devotional books and by priests. Different texts and regions do not always agree, so treat this as a starting map rather than a fixed rule.
list: One mukhi: Shiva himself. A truly round one mukhi bead is considered extremely rare.
Two mukhi: Ardhanarishvara, the combined form of Shiva and Parvati, which is why it is often linked with partnership.
Three mukhi: Agni, the fire deity.
Four mukhi: Brahma, and through him learning and speech. Some families give it to students.
Five mukhi: Kalagni Rudra, a form of Shiva. This is the most common bead and the standard choice for japa malas.
Six mukhi: Kartikeya, the son of Shiva and Parvati.
Seven mukhi: most often Goddess Mahalakshmi, though some accounts connect it with the Saptarishis.

sections.heading: Eight to fourteen mukhi, and two special forms
paragraphs: Higher counts are rarer, so you will mostly see them sold as single beads rather than full malas.
list: Eight mukhi: Lord Ganesha.
Nine mukhi: Goddess Durga, and the nine forms worshipped during Navratri.
Ten mukhi: Lord Vishnu.
Eleven mukhi: the eleven Rudras, and in many accounts Hanuman.
Twelve mukhi: Surya, the sun deity.
Thirteen mukhi: varies by text; Kamadeva and Indra are both mentioned.
Fourteen mukhi: linked with Hanuman in some traditions and with Shiva in others.
Gauri Shankar: two beads naturally joined together, seen as Shiva and Parvati united.
Ganesh rudraksha: a bead with a small trunk-like bump on its surface.

sections.heading: Why the five mukhi bead is everywhere
paragraphs: Five mukhi beads grow in far greater numbers than any other kind, which keeps them affordable and easy to match in size for a full string. That is why almost every japa mala you see in a temple shop is made of five mukhi beads. Many traditions also consider the five mukhi suitable for anyone, with no special conditions attached, so it is the usual recommendation for a first mala.

Some astrologers pair individual mukhis with planets and suggest a bead based on a birth chart. These pairings differ from one practitioner to another, and they are a matter of belief. If you follow such advice, it is worth asking a person you trust rather than relying on a product listing.

sections.heading: Reading seller claims with a clear head
paragraphs: Because rarer beads cost more, they attract imitations. Common tricks include extra lines carved into a lower-mukhi bead, two beads glued to look like a Gauri Shankar, and beads moulded from resin or wood. Popular home tests, such as dropping a bead in water to see if it sinks, are not reliable and should not be used to judge a costly bead.
list: Count the lines yourself before paying, and look for any line that suddenly changes depth or direction.
Check the joint on a two-bead piece under a magnifier for traces of glue.
Treat any listing that promises a specific outcome from a bead with caution.
For a high-value single bead, buy only where you can return it and get a second opinion.

sections.heading: Where chain-style malas fit in
paragraphs: Not every rudraksha piece is bought for its mukhi count. A lot of people simply want a devotional necklace to wear on Mondays, on festival days or every day. For that, the look, the pendant and the comfort of the chain matter more than the exact number of lines. The [rudraksha chain malas at Varaha](/divine) are made for this kind of wear: fashion and devotional necklaces with rudraksha beads and gold-plated Om, Trishul, Ganesha or Shiva pendants, sold without any mukhi grading or certification.

faq.q: Which mukhi rudraksha is best for beginners?
faq.a: Most traditions suggest the five mukhi bead for a first mala, as it is common, affordable and considered suitable for everyone.

faq.q: Is one mukhi rudraksha easy to find?
faq.a: A round one mukhi bead is considered very rare, so be cautious of low-priced listings that claim to be one.

faq.q: Can I wear different mukhi beads together?
faq.a: Many people do, and some malas mix counts by design. Customs vary, so check with an elder or priest if you follow a specific practice.
